title: Understanding Menopause
description: Understand menopause, common symptoms, when to seek medical advice and how a GP can help you review treatment and long-term health.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Menopause is more than the final menstrual period
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Understanding Menopause Understand menopause, common symptoms, when to seek medical advice and how a GP can help you review treatment and long-term health. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Menopause is a normal life stage, but the transition can affect people very differently. Symptoms may begin during perimenopause and can include hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disturbance, mood changes, vaginal or urinary symptoms and changes in periods. Why This Topic Matters Menopause is confirmed after 12 months without a menstrual period, provided there is no other explanation. The transition can affect sleep, temperature regulation, sexual wellbeing and longer-term bone health; experiences vary widely. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, mood changes and interrupted sleep are common reasons for discussion. Unexplained bleeding after menopause needs assessment rather than attribution to hormonal change. Symptoms interfere with sleep, work or relationships. You develop bleeding after 12 months without a period. You want to weigh hormone therapy and non-hormonal options against personal risks. Menopause is more than the final menstrual period Menopause is reached after 12 months without a menstrual period when there is no other explanation. The years leading up to it are called perimenopause, when periods and symptoms can become less predictable. A useful consultation looks at symptoms, age, menstrual history, contraception needs, personal and family history, cardiovascular and bone health, medicines and what matters most to you. Treatment is individual and may include lifestyle measures, non-hormonal options or menopause hormone therapy when appropriate. Keep a record of symptoms and menstrual changes if helpful Discuss abnormal or unexpected bleeding rather than assuming it is menopause Ask about contraception until menopause is confirmed Review bone, heart and preventive health as part of midlife care When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book medical advice if symptoms are affecting sleep, mood, work, relationships or quality of life. Any vaginal bleeding after menopause should be medically assessed. Severe or rapidly worsening symptoms also deserve prompt review. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess symptoms, consider other possible causes, discuss treatment choices and contraindications, review preventive health, and refer to a gynaecologist or other clinician when specialist input is appropriate. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between perimenopause and menopause? Perimenopause is the transition leading up to menopause. Menopause is confirmed after 12 months without a period when there is no other cause. Do I always need a blood test to diagnose menopause? Not always. In many people the diagnosis is based on age, symptoms and menstrual history. Testing may be useful in particular circumstances. Can a GP discuss menopause hormone therapy? Yes. A GP can discuss potential benefits, risks and alternatives and determine whether further assessment or specialist input is needed. title: Cervical Screening Guide
h1: When Should I Have A Cervical Screening Test?
description: Learn about cervical screening intervals in Australia, self-collection and when symptoms need medical assessment.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Routine screening and symptom assessment are not the same thing
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should i have a cervical screening test
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health When Should I Have A Cervical Screening Test? Understand current Australian cervical screening intervals, self-collection options and when symptoms need assessment rather than routine screening. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Australia’s National Cervical Screening Program uses HPV testing to reduce the risk of cervical cancer. For most eligible women and people with a cervix aged 25 to 74, routine screening is recommended every five years, but individual circumstances can change what is appropriate. Why This Topic Matters Cervical screening looks for HPV associated with cervical cancer, rather than waiting for symptoms. Under the National Cervical Screening Program, most eligible people with a cervix aged 25–74 are invited every five years; individual follow-up can differ after an abnormal result. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Routine screening is intended for people without symptoms. Bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods, bleeding after menopause or unusual persistent discharge warrants assessment even if your screening is up to date. You are due for routine screening or unsure when your last test was. You would like to discuss self-collection and clinician collection. You have symptoms that need diagnostic assessment, not just routine screening. Routine screening and symptom assessment are not the same thing The Cervical Screening Test checks for human papillomavirus (HPV), which can cause cervical cell changes. Eligible participants can discuss clinician-collected and self-collected sampling options with their healthcare provider. Routine screening is designed for people without symptoms. Symptoms such as unusual vaginal bleeding, bleeding after sex, persistent unusual discharge or pelvic symptoms should be discussed with a clinician even if your next routine screening test is not due. Most eligible participants are invited from age 25 to 74 Routine interval is generally five years when previous results and circumstances allow Self-collection is an option for eligible participants under the national program Previous abnormal results, immune conditions or other clinical factors can change follow-up When Should I Seek Medical Advice? See a GP if you are unsure when you are due, have received an abnormal result, have symptoms such as unusual bleeding or discharge, or need help choosing a collection option. Significant bleeding, severe pain or rapidly worsening symptoms may need urgent assessment. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can confirm your screening history, explain current eligibility, arrange or perform screening, discuss self-collection, interpret results and coordinate follow-up or specialist referral if needed. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions Is the Cervical Screening Test the same as the old Pap smear? The current program primarily tests for HPV rather than looking first for abnormal cells, although people still commonly use the term Pap smear. Can I collect my own sample? Eligible participants can choose self-collection under the National Cervical Screening Program. Your healthcare provider can explain whether it is suitable for you. Should I wait for my screening date if I have symptoms? No. Symptoms need clinical assessment and should not be delayed until the next routine screening test. h1: Women's Health Checks At Different Stages Of Life
description: Explore women's health checks across life stages, including screening, vaccination, reproductive and midlife care.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Preventive care changes as your priorities change
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles womens health checks at different stages of life
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Women's Health Checks At Different Stages Of Life A stage-by-stage guide to preventive women’s healthcare, including screening, reproductive health, vaccination and midlife health discussions. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction There is no single ‘women’s health check’ that is right for everyone. Preventive care changes with age, symptoms, reproductive plans, family history, previous results and health risks. Why This Topic Matters Preventive priorities change with age, pregnancy plans, medications, medical history and personal circumstances. A useful review addresses individual risk rather than giving every patient the same package of tests. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Discussions may involve menstrual health, contraception, pregnancy planning, cervical screening, cardiovascular risk, menopause symptoms or bone health. Family history can change screening and referral decisions. You are planning pregnancy or considering contraception. You have new menstrual, breast or menopause symptoms. Your family history or screening status has changed. Preventive care changes as your priorities change In younger adulthood, consultations may focus on contraception, sexual health, vaccination, mental health and cervical screening when eligible. Pregnancy planning can add folate, medicines review, vaccination and chronic condition optimisation. Midlife care may include menopause symptoms, cardiovascular risk, bone health and screening. Later-life care can increasingly focus on mobility, medicines, chronic conditions, falls risk, vaccination and maintaining independence. Cervical screening according to the national program Breast awareness and age-appropriate breast screening discussions Blood pressure and cardiovascular risk assessment Vaccination and sexual health when relevant Pregnancy planning, menopause or healthy ageing according to life stage When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a GP appointment if you are unsure which preventive checks apply to you, have new symptoms, have a strong family history or are entering a new life stage such as pregnancy planning or menopause. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review your individual risk profile and screening history, identify what is due, avoid unnecessary testing, discuss prevention and coordinate referrals to screening programs or specialists where appropriate. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need an annual full blood test? Not necessarily. Tests should be based on symptoms, age, risk factors and clinical need rather than a fixed yearly panel for everyone. Are screening programs the same for every person? No. National programs provide age and risk guidance, but previous results, symptoms and individual history may alter recommendations. Can preventive care be discussed during a routine GP visit? Yes. Depending on time and complexity, your GP can review prevention during a routine visit or recommend a dedicated longer appointment. title: Perimenopause Guide
description: Learn what perimenopause is, common symptoms, when to see a GP and how treatment and contraception can be discussed.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Perimenopause can affect periods, sleep, mood and wellbeing
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Understanding Perimenopause Learn what perimenopause is, common symptoms, when to see a GP and how treatment and contraception can be discussed. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Perimenopause is the transition before menopause. Hormone levels can fluctuate, periods may change and symptoms can come and go for several years. Because the pattern varies widely, care should be guided by the individual rather than a fixed list of symptoms. Why This Topic Matters Perimenopause is the time of hormonal change leading up to menopause. Cycle changes may begin years before the final period, and pregnancy remains possible while ovulation continues. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Periods may become irregular, heavier or lighter; hot flushes, headaches, sleep disruption and mood changes may occur. Very heavy bleeding, bleeding between periods or bleeding after sex should be assessed independently of age. Bleeding becomes heavy, prolonged or unpredictable. Symptoms affect wellbeing or you are uncertain about contraception. You are younger than expected for menopause or have new symptoms needing assessment. Perimenopause can affect periods, sleep, mood and wellbeing Common experiences include changes in menstrual timing or flow, hot flushes, night sweats, sleep problems, vaginal dryness, mood changes, anxiety, reduced concentration and joint or muscle symptoms. Pregnancy is still possible during perimenopause. Contraception, pregnancy intentions and treatment choices should therefore be considered together. Symptoms under age 45, very heavy bleeding or unusual bleeding patterns may need additional assessment. Track period changes and symptoms if this helps identify a pattern Do not assume every symptom is hormonal Discuss contraception while pregnancy remains possible Raise heavy, prolonged or otherwise unusual bleeding with a clinician When Should I Seek Medical Advice? See a GP if symptoms are difficult to manage, affect daily life, begin unusually early, or if bleeding is heavy, prolonged, occurs after sex or is otherwise concerning. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess whether symptoms fit perimenopause, consider alternative explanations, discuss contraception and treatment options, and review longer-term bone, heart and preventive health. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions Can perimenopause start while I still have regular periods? Symptoms can begin before periods stop completely, although menstrual changes are common as the transition progresses. Can I still become pregnant during perimenopause? Yes. Pregnancy remains possible until menopause is confirmed, so discuss contraception if you do not want to become pregnant. Are hormone blood tests always needed? No. Assessment is often based on age, symptoms and menstrual history. Testing is more useful in selected circumstances. title: Women's Preventive Care
description: Explore women's preventive care, including screening, vaccination, heart health, reproductive care and mental wellbeing.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise
Prevention works best when care is connected
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Preventive Women's Healthcare Understand how preventive women’s healthcare brings together screening, vaccination, cardiovascular health, reproductive care and mental wellbeing. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Preventive women’s healthcare is not a single appointment or test. It is an ongoing process of matching screening, vaccination and risk reduction to your age, history, symptoms and life stage. Why This Topic Matters Prevention includes screening when eligible, vaccination, addressing lifestyle risks and acting on symptoms. Tests without a clear indication may cause unnecessary worry or follow-up, so decisions should be individualised. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Relevant situations include overdue cervical screening, questions about breast screening, changes in blood pressure, diabetes risks and vaccination planning. A new symptom requires its own assessment; screening is not a substitute. You are unsure which screening invitations apply to your age. You have strong family history of cancer, heart disease or diabetes. You are entering a new life stage and want to review health priorities. Prevention works best when care is connected A GP can help bring together cervical screening, breast health, blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, vaccination, sexual and reproductive health, mental wellbeing, pregnancy planning, menopause and healthy ageing. The aim is not to perform every possible test. It is to identify what is recommended, what is clinically useful now and what can safely wait, while keeping future follow-up visible. Keep screening and vaccination history up to date Review medicines before pregnancy or when health circumstances change Discuss family history that may alter screening decisions Use routine visits to revisit prevention over time When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a preventive health discussion if you are unsure what is due, have missed screening, have a significant family history or are preparing for pregnancy, menopause or another life transition. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can personalise prevention, check national screening recommendations, assess risk factors, discuss lifestyle and reproductive health, and arrange tests or referrals that are clinically indicated. Woolloongabba Medical Centre supports women's healthcare for patients across Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and surrounding inner-south communities. Frequently Asked Questions What should a preventive health appointment include? It depends on your age and individual risks. It may include screening history, blood pressure, vaccination, lifestyle, reproductive health and other targeted checks. Is more testing always better? No. Preventive care aims for appropriate evidence-based screening and risk assessment, not indiscriminate testing. Can family history change what I need? Yes. Some family histories can change the timing or type of screening, so tell your GP about important conditions in close relatives. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Women's Health Breast Health: Changes, Screening & When To See A GP Learn which breast changes need assessment, how BreastScreen Australia works and why symptoms need diagnostic review. Introduction Breast health involves understanding what is normal for your body, noticing changes and using screening appropriately. A new breast symptom should be assessed even if a recent screening mammogram was normal; screening and investigating symptoms serve different purposes. Why This Topic Matters BreastScreen Australia invites eligible women aged 50–74 for a free mammogram every two years. Women aged 40–49 and 75 or older may also access free screening, but are generally not routinely invited. Family history and symptoms may change the recommended pathway. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: A new lump or thickened area in a breast or armpit. Nipple discharge, especially if bloody, or a newly inverted nipple. Persistent skin dimpling, redness, swelling or a change in breast shape. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Arrange a GP appointment promptly for a new lump, persistent breast change or unexplained nipple discharge. Do not wait for the next routine BreastScreen invitation. Sudden severe infection symptoms or rapidly worsening illness may require urgent care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can take a history, examine the area, review family risk and arrange appropriate imaging or referral when indicated. Your clinician can also explain routine screening eligibility. Screening mammograms are not a substitute for diagnostic investigation of a new symptom. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need to wait until age 50 for a breast screen? Women aged 40–49 may access free BreastScreen mammography, but screening decisions should take individual risks into account. I had a normal mammogram. Should I ignore a new lump? No. A new lump or change requires assessment even after normal screening. Are all breast lumps cancer? No. Many are benign, but examination and, where needed, imaging are important to identify the cause. title: Healthy Ageing: Falls, Vaccines & GP Reviews
h1: Healthy Ageing: Prevention, Falls, Vaccination & Reviews
description: Practical healthy-ageing advice about fall prevention, vaccination, medicines and GP health reviews for older adults.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles healthy ageing prevention falls vaccination reviews
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Healthy Ageing Healthy Ageing: Prevention, Falls, Vaccination & Reviews Practical healthy-ageing advice about fall prevention, vaccination, medicines and GP health reviews for older adults. Introduction Healthy ageing is about staying as well and independent as possible, not simply treating diseases after they appear. Changes in strength, balance, hearing, memory or medicines can affect everyday activities, so preventive reviews should consider the whole person. Why This Topic Matters Falls can lead to injuries and loss of confidence, while complex medicine regimens can increase side effects. Vaccinations and age-appropriate screening can reduce specific risks. Plans work best when they reflect the person's own priorities, living circumstances and support network. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: A recent fall, near-fall, dizziness or new hesitation about walking outdoors. Unexpected weight loss, reduced strength, memory concerns or difficulty managing medicines. Uncertainty about influenza, shingles, pneumococcal and other recommended vaccinations. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a GP review after a fall, when daily function is changing, or when a medicine causes dizziness or confusion. Sudden weakness on one side, facial droop, new speech difficulty or acute confusion may indicate an emergency: call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess fall risks, blood pressure, vision and medicine effects, discuss exercise and bone health, and consider physiotherapy or other support. They may recommend a relevant health assessment, personalised vaccination review or tests based on medical history. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Are falls just part of getting older? No. Falls have many potential contributors, and identifying modifiable risks can make a difference. Should older people have a medicine review? A review is especially useful after falls, side effects, hospital discharge or multiple prescription changes. Is every vaccine funded for all older adults? No. Recommendations and National Immunisation Program funding depend on age and other eligibility criteria. description: A pre-pregnancy appointment can identify health needs before conception.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Pregnancy & Antenatal Care Planning A Pregnancy A pre-pregnancy appointment can identify health needs before conception. It can be useful whether you are ready to try now or are thinking about pregnancy in the coming months. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction A pre-pregnancy appointment can identify health needs before conception. It can be useful whether you are ready to try now or are thinking about pregnancy in the coming months. What Is It? Preconception care may include reviewing medicines, vaccination status, chronic conditions, family history, lifestyle and any previous pregnancy complications. Folic acid before and in early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural-tube defects; iodine advice depends on circumstances including thyroid health. Regular medicine review before pregnancy Past pregnancy complications Questions about supplements and screening Should I Be Concerned? Arrange an appointment if you take regular medicines, have diabetes, high blood pressure, epilepsy or a mental health condition, have difficulty conceiving, or have a history of miscarriage. Do not stop essential medication abruptly when planning pregnancy. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Severe pelvic pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or suspected ectopic pregnancy symptoms require immediate emergency evaluation. Once pregnant, severe pain or significant bleeding should not wait for a routine review. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can discuss preconception blood tests where indicated, folic acid and iodine, genetic or carrier screening options, medicine safety and referral if fertility concerns or higher-risk pregnancy factors are present. Bring any relevant pregnancy tests, your medicine list and questions about early pregnancy care and maternity referrals. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions When should I start folic acid? Australian guidance recommends taking folic acid before conception and during early pregnancy; some people need a higher dose. Ask your GP for a personal recommendation. Do I need to update vaccinations before pregnancy? Some vaccines are best given before conception and others during pregnancy. A GP can review your record and current Australian recommendations. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. title: What Happens During Antenatal Care?
description: Antenatal appointments monitor the health of the pregnant person and baby, answer questions and help identify concerns early.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles what happens during antenatal care
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Pregnancy & Antenatal Care What Happens During Antenatal Care? Antenatal care is a series of appointments designed to monitor the health of the pregnant person and baby, answer questions and identify concerns early. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Antenatal care is a series of appointments designed to monitor the health of the pregnant person and baby, answer questions and identify concerns early. What Is It? Care may involve a GP, midwife, obstetrician and hospital maternity team. Visits can include blood pressure checks, blood tests, ultrasound referrals, discussion of screening options, vaccines, medicines, nutrition and emotional wellbeing. The schedule depends on pregnancy stage and risk. Planning scans and screening Questions about medicines or vaccination Bleeding, severe symptoms or changes in pregnancy wellbeing Should I Be Concerned? Contact your maternity care provider for bleeding, persistent vomiting, new swelling, severe headache, unusual pain or changes in your baby’s movements once movements are established. Do not wait for the next booked visit if you are concerned. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 for heavy bleeding with collapse, seizures or other life-threatening symptoms. For urgent pregnancy problems, contact your maternity assessment unit or emergency department according to your stage of pregnancy and local arrangements. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can help establish a maternity care pathway, provide shared antenatal care where appropriate, review other health conditions and coordinate referrals. Confirm which appointments and services your chosen GP provides before booking. Bring any relevant pregnancy tests, your medicine list and questions about early pregnancy care and maternity referrals. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Will I only see a GP during pregnancy? Not usually. Australian maternity care commonly involves a hospital, midwifery or obstetric team alongside GP care. Can I ask about emotional wellbeing? Yes. Mood, anxiety, sleep and support at home are important parts of pregnancy care and can be discussed at antenatal visits. title: First Pregnancy GP Appointment
description: A first pregnancy visit is an opportunity to confirm next steps and ask questions.

text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Pregnancy & Antenatal Care Your First Pregnancy GP Appointment A first pregnancy visit is an opportunity to confirm next steps and ask questions. You do not need to know all the tests or make every decision before attending. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction A first pregnancy visit is an opportunity to confirm next steps and ask questions. You do not need to know all the tests or make every decision before attending. What Is It? Your GP may ask about the date of your last period, medical and family history, medicines, previous pregnancies and any symptoms. They may discuss blood tests, ultrasound timing, screening choices, nutrition and local maternity services. Positive home pregnancy test Questions about first-trimester screening Medication or previous pregnancy concerns Should I Be Concerned? Book when you know or suspect you are pregnant so care can be planned early. In Australia, the first antenatal review is commonly arranged around six to eight weeks, but earlier assessment may be needed with pain, bleeding or relevant medical conditions. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Severe one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or heavy bleeding may suggest an emergency including ectopic pregnancy; seek emergency care immediately. Call 000 if there is collapse or severe symptoms. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can explain test choices, discuss supplements and medication safety, confirm relevant referral pathways and make sure ongoing pregnancy care is organised. Bringing your medication list and questions can help. Bring any relevant pregnancy tests, your medicine list and questions about early pregnancy care and maternity referrals. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need an ultrasound before the first GP visit? No. A GP can discuss whether and when an ultrasound is appropriate for your situation. Can I continue my usual medicines? Some are safe and others need adjustment. Ask promptly for individual advice, and do not stop essential medicines without medical guidance. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. title: Healthy Weight Management
description: Weight and health are connected, but a number on the scale does not describe the whole person.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Weight & Healthy Lifestyle Healthy Weight Management Weight and health are connected, but a number on the scale does not describe the whole person. A helpful plan focuses on wellbeing, sustainable habits and any medical issues affecting weight. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Weight and health are connected, but a number on the scale does not describe the whole person. A helpful plan focuses on wellbeing, sustainable habits and any medical issues affecting weight. What Is It? Body weight can be influenced by genetics, medicines, sleep, hormones, living circumstances, activity and food access. Evidence-based care avoids blame and extreme dieting, and considers blood pressure, blood glucose, cholesterol, mobility and quality of life. Weight affecting blood pressure or diabetes Unexplained weight change Questions about evidence-based support Should I Be Concerned? Book a conversation if weight changes unexpectedly, affects health or movement, or if repeated attempts to change weight have been distressing. Rapid unintentional weight loss, persistent fatigue or other symptoms deserve medical review rather than a diet plan alone. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Sudden weight changes with severe illness, confusion, dehydration or other emergency symptoms require urgent assessment. Weight management appointments are not a substitute for treatment of acute illness or disordered eating symptoms that threaten safety. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess relevant health risks and possible medical contributors, review medicines and work with you on realistic goals. Options may include dietitian or exercise-physiology support, sleep assessment or medicines when clinically indicated. You can discuss your own health priorities, medicines, activity limits and what changes feel realistic without judgement. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is there one best diet for everyone? No. A sustainable approach that meets nutritional needs and fits a person’s circumstances is preferable to rigid fad diets. Will my GP prescribe weight-loss medicines? Medicines may be considered for some patients after assessment of indications, benefits, risks and alternatives; they are not suitable for everyone. title: When Should I Speak To A GP About Weight?
h1: When Should I Speak To A GP About Weight?
description: You can raise weight concerns with a GP without waiting for a crisis or a particular body-mass-index result.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should i speak to a gp about weight
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Weight & Healthy Lifestyle When Should I Speak To A GP About Weight? You can raise weight concerns with a GP without waiting for a crisis or a particular body-mass-index result. The conversation should be respectful and related to your own health goals. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction You can raise weight concerns with a GP without waiting for a crisis or a particular body-mass-index result. The conversation should be respectful and related to your own health goals. What Is It? Changes in weight may reflect food and activity patterns, medicines, sleep, stress or health conditions. A useful appointment considers not only weight but your medical history, metabolism, mood and whether eating behaviours are becoming distressing. Unexpected weight changes Concern about restrictive diets Weight affecting mobility or long-term health Should I Be Concerned? Arrange a visit for unplanned gain or loss, weight-related joint pain or breathlessness, diabetes risk, or concerns about restrictive eating. Tell your GP if you would prefer not to have your weight announced during the consultation. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Severe dehydration, fainting, chest pain or acute illness require urgent care. If food restriction, purging or an eating disorder is affecting physical safety, seek prompt medical assessment rather than following generic weight advice. How Can a GP Help? A GP can ask permission before discussing weight, arrange targeted tests if needed and offer a health-focused plan. Referrals may include a dietitian, psychologist or other professional depending on the circumstances. You can discuss your own health priorities, medicines, activity limits and what changes feel realistic without judgement. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Will every consultation involve a weigh-in? Not necessarily. Explain your preferences and ask how a measurement would affect clinical decisions. Can medicines affect weight? Yes. Several medicines and medical conditions can influence weight. A GP can review possible contributors without stopping treatment abruptly. title: Understanding Healthy Lifestyle Changes
description: Health advice can feel overwhelming. Useful lifestyle changes are specific, achievable and reviewed over time with support from your GP.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles understanding healthy lifestyle changes
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Weight & Healthy Lifestyle Understanding Healthy Lifestyle Changes Health advice can feel overwhelming when it is presented as a long list of rules. The most useful changes are specific, achievable and revisited over time. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Health advice can feel overwhelming when it is presented as a long list of rules. The most useful changes are specific, achievable and revisited over time. What Is It? Healthy lifestyle habits include food variety, movement, sleep, stress management, avoiding tobacco and moderating alcohol. Their benefits extend beyond weight to cardiovascular health, mental wellbeing, mobility and diabetes prevention. Starting movement after inactivity Questions about healthy eating patterns Managing sleep and stress alongside health goals Should I Be Concerned? Talk to a GP if health advice conflicts with a medical condition, medicines or physical limits, or if you are unsure where to begin. Breathlessness, persistent fatigue, pain or mood changes may need assessment before a new exercise plan. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Chest pain, fainting during exertion or severe breathlessness requires urgent assessment; call 000 for life-threatening symptoms. A new activity routine should not be used to push through significant warning signs. How Can a GP Help? A GP can prioritise one or two changes that matter for your health, check risk factors and refer for tailored support. Setting a realistic follow-up date is often more valuable than making a dramatic change that cannot be sustained. You can discuss your own health priorities, medicines, activity limits and what changes feel realistic without judgement. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Do I have to change everything at once? No. Gradual and consistent changes are often easier to maintain, especially when supported by realistic goals. Is exercise safe with a chronic condition? Often yes, but the type and intensity should be tailored to your condition, medicines and current fitness. title: Menopause Symptoms Explained
description: Menopause is a natural stage of life, but symptoms can interfere with sleep, work and wellbeing.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Menopause & Midlife Health Menopause Symptoms Explained Menopause is a natural stage of life, but symptoms can interfere with sleep, work and wellbeing. People experience different combinations of symptoms and not everyone needs treatment. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Menopause is a natural stage of life, but symptoms can interfere with sleep, work and wellbeing. People experience different combinations of symptoms and not everyone needs treatment. What Is It? Menopause is defined retrospectively after twelve months without a menstrual period in a person not using hormonal treatment that changes bleeding. Perimenopause is the transition leading up to that point. Hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disturbance, vaginal dryness, mood changes and irregular cycles can occur. Hot flushes and night sweats Irregular bleeding or vaginal symptoms Sleep and mood changes around midlife Should I Be Concerned? Arrange a GP appointment if symptoms affect quality of life, if bleeding is heavy or unusual, or if periods stop unusually early. New bleeding after menopause needs assessment rather than being assumed to be a normal hormonal change. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Severe bleeding with fainting or collapse requires urgent assessment. Chest pain, stroke-like symptoms or severe breathlessness are emergencies: call 000. Do not explain every new symptom as menopause without considering other causes. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review the symptom pattern and health history, discuss non-hormonal strategies and menopausal hormone therapy where appropriate, and assess other health considerations such as bone and heart health. Notes about menstrual changes, sleep, hot flushes and how symptoms affect your day can help guide a personalised discussion. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Do I always need a hormone blood test? Not always. For many people over 45, the symptom and menstrual history is more useful than a single hormone result. Can symptoms start before periods stop? Yes. Perimenopause can involve symptoms and irregular bleeding before the final menstrual period. Deciding whether it is suitable should be a shared discussion rather than a standard prescription for everyone. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Menopausal hormone therapy, sometimes called HRT, may help with troublesome menopausal symptoms. Deciding whether it is suitable should be a shared discussion rather than a standard prescription for everyone. What Is It? Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) can relieve hot flushes, night sweats and some vaginal symptoms. Options include patches, gels, tablets and local vaginal treatments. People with a uterus who use systemic oestrogen usually need endometrial protection with a progestogen. Persistent hot flushes or night sweats Questions about patches or vaginal treatment Reviewing hormone therapy risks and side effects Should I Be Concerned? Speak with a GP if symptoms significantly affect sleep or daily activities, you are considering MHT or you have questions about alternatives. Personal factors such as clotting history, unexplained bleeding, cardiovascular disease and certain cancers influence suitability. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Unexpected heavy bleeding, severe chest pain, stroke symptoms or sudden breathlessness require urgent care. If you develop symptoms suggesting a blood clot while using hormone therapy, seek immediate medical assessment. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review benefits, risks, preparation type and dose, as well as alternatives and follow-up. Regular reassessment considers symptom benefit, side effects, medical history and changing preferences; MHT is not prescribed solely to prevent chronic disease. Notes about menstrual changes, sleep, hot flushes and how symptoms affect your day can help guide a personalised discussion. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is HRT suitable for everyone? No. Benefits and risks depend on age, medical history, type of hormone treatment and personal circumstances. Are patches and tablets identical? No. Routes of administration have different considerations, including clotting risk, which your GP can explain. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Menopause & Midlife Health Mental Health & Menopause Mood changes during midlife can be confusing, particularly when they happen alongside disrupted sleep and physical menopausal symptoms. The connection deserves assessment without assuming hormones explain everything. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Mood changes during midlife can be confusing, particularly when they happen alongside disrupted sleep and physical menopausal symptoms. The connection deserves assessment without assuming hormones explain everything. What Is It? Hormonal changes during perimenopause may coincide with anxiety, irritability, low mood, reduced concentration or sleep problems. Work, caregiving, previous mental health conditions and other medical factors can also influence how a person feels. Mood changes with hot flushes Difficulty sleeping and concentrating Persistent anxiety, irritability or low mood Should I Be Concerned? Book an appointment if mood or anxiety symptoms persist, interfere with relationships or work, or affect your ability to cope. Share sleep changes, menstrual history, medicines and whether symptoms occur alongside hot flushes or night sweats. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? If you are at immediate risk of harming yourself or another person, call 000 or attend an emergency department. New severe confusion, chest pain or major physical symptoms must not be attributed to menopause alone. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review mental and physical health together, discuss talking therapies, sleep support, non-hormonal treatment and whether MHT may help menopausal symptoms. Follow-up is important to assess what is improving and what still needs care. Notes about menstrual changes, sleep, hot flushes and how symptoms affect your day can help guide a personalised discussion. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can menopause cause anxiety? Hormonal changes and sleep disruption may contribute, but anxiety can have other causes that also deserve assessment. Can I discuss mental health and menopause in one GP appointment? Yes. Ask reception whether a longer appointment would allow enough time for a fuller discussion.
